title: How can "tree" and "truth" be related? | WOODLAND WORDS

entries.note: From a Monty Python sketch: words that sound satisfying, like gorse, caribou and wasp, set against [[see:tiny words]].
In the Monty Python sketch, the less pleasant-sounding words, such as newspaper, set against [[see:woody words]].
Old English word meaning a tree, a grove, a forest or the material; it could also mean wild, and was used for mad animals before 'mad'.
Via French from Latin forestis silva, the outside woods set aside for royal hunting; [[see:silva]] meant the forest, and forestis just meant outside.
The part of Latin forestis silva that actually meant forest, also found in [[see:Pennsylvania]] and [[see:Transylvania]].
A name containing Latin [[from:silva]], forest.
Means beyond the woods, from Latin [[from:silva]], so roughly the same idea as [[see:forest]].
Related to [[same-root:forest]] through the idea of outside, so a foreigner is someone from outside.
Once a fenced game preserve on royal land, as opposed to the unfenced, outside [[see:forest]]; now used for public and national parks.
From Old English, helped by a similar Old Norse word; traced to a PIE root meaning steadfast, shared with [[same-root:true]] and [[same-root:durable]].
Thought to share a PIE root meaning steadfast with [[same-root:tree]].
Thought to share a PIE root meaning steadfast with [[same-root:tree]].
The German word for tree, an example of the usual West Germanic word that English [[see:tree]] does not reflect.
Scientific term meaning tree-like, from the same PIE root as [[same-root:tree]].
Dating by trees, for example by counting their rings; from the same PIE root as [[same-root:tree]].
Means rose tree, and contains the same PIE root as [[same-root:tree]].
Means tree-loving because it grows next to trees, and contains the same root as [[same-root:tree]].
Enduring is another word from the same PIE root as [[same-root:tree]].
A wood nymph or nymph of the trees, from the same root as [[same-root:tree]].
Borrowed from Old Norse, not Old English; related to [[same-root:birch]]. Old English used [[see:rind]] instead.
From French and ultimately Latin, meaning the body of a tree; related to [[same-root:trump]], a hollow tube.
The old name for a [[see:trumpet]], a hollow tube; in British English it also means a fart, which amuses Brits given [[see:Donald Trump]].
Was originally called a [[see:trump]].
The US president, whose surname Brits find funny because [[see:trump]] means fart in British English.
From Latin [[from:branca]], an animal's paw, much like a limb.
Another word for an arm that is also used for the [[see:branch]] of a tree.
Old Germanic word meaning fork, since twigs fork off.
Simply means leaf; its plural 'leaves' shows the old English F-to-V change between vowels, as with [[see:wolf]] and [[see:knife]].
Its plural wolves shows the same F-to-V change as [[see:leaf]].
Its plural knives shows the same F-to-V change as [[see:leaf]], discussed before.
The usual Germanic word for a leaf, also meaning a page; related to [[same-root:blade]].
The Danish word for a leaf, like German [[same-root:Blatt]].
Related to the Germanic leaf words [[same-root:Blatt]] and [[same-root:blad]].
Once a synonym for leaf, from French [[from:feuille]], a leaf or thin sheet; survives in metallic tin foil.
Sometimes mispronounced 'foilage', which isn't entirely wrong since the word entered from French in a form close to [[same-root:foil]].
A collection of leaves or papers, as with Shakespeare's pages, linking tree leaves with book leaves.
German business newspaper whose name contains [[see:Blatt]] in the sense of page.
Named after a writing material: same root as [[same-root:beech]], because early tablets were often beechwood.
Shares a root with [[same-root:book]], because early tablets were made of beechwood; unrelated to [[unrelated:birch]].
Related to [[same-root:bark]] and to Icelandic [[same-root:Björk]]; it also named the rune for B.
The singer's name is simply the Icelandic for [[same-root:birch]].
The Old English word for tree [[see:bark]], like orange rind; in German Rind means beef.
The woody part of a plant, coined alongside [[see:phloem]] in the late 1800s from Greek for wood, which also gave [[same-root:xylophone]].
Coined alongside [[see:xylem]] from the Greek for bark; [[see:fluid]] is linked through a Latin word for to flow.
From the Greek for wood, like [[same-root:xylem]]: a way to remember it's the wooden one, unlike the [[see:glockenspiel]].
Means bell play in German, unlike the wooden [[see:xylophone]].
From the Latin for to flow, which the hosts link to [[see:phloem]].
Means that which falls down, from Latin cadere, to fall, like [[same-root:cascade]] and [[same-root:decay]]; unrelated to [[unrelated:decide]].
Shares the root meaning to fall with [[same-root:deciduous]].
Something that befalls you; shares the root meaning to fall with [[same-root:deciduous]].
Implies morally falling; shares the root meaning to fall with [[same-root:deciduous]].
Shares the root meaning to fall with [[same-root:deciduous]].
Looks like [[unrelated:deciduous]] but comes from a root meaning to cut, cutting away an option, as in other -cide words.
Means cone-bearing; not all conifers are evergreen, like [[see:larch]]es and the [[see:Chinese swamp cypress]].
An example of a conifer that is not evergreen.
A deciduous conifer, an example of conifers that are not evergreen.
Also called water pine, a deciduous conifer; jokingly both from a Chinese swamp and from Cyprus, though it may not be a true cypress.
Its link with Cyprus was covered in a previous episode.
Means fat, sharing a PIE root with [[same-root:Ireland]], perhaps because pine-forested land was fertile.
An old Germanic word that simply means oak; it also named a rune.
Like [[see:beaver]], a name meaning brown, unlike [[see:oak]].
Literally fertile or fat land, from the same PIE root as [[same-root:pine]].
Basically just means maple.
A very old word for several trees, perhaps implying movement from its quaking leaves; Old English called it [[see:quickbeam]].
The Colorado place is named after the [[from:aspen]] tree.
An aspen grove, probably in Utah, said to be the largest organism on the planet because its trees share one root system.
Old English name for the [[see:aspen]], meaning moving tree, from [[from:quick]] in its sense of moving.
Discussed before as meaning moving, as in [[see:quicksilver]] and [[see:quickbeam]].
An example of [[see:quick]] meaning moving.
Has always basically been called an ash, and named a [[see:rune]].
Has always been called something like yew, and named a [[see:rune]].
Rob made a video on runes: unlike modern letters they had meaningful names such as [[see:oak]], [[see:ash]], [[see:yew]] and [[see:birch]], showing the trees' importance.
Nothing to do with dogs: originally dag tree, a stabbing tree, used for butchers' skewers, like a [[see:dagger]].
Something you dag, or stab, with, like the original dag tree behind [[see:dogwood]].
Not from looking furry: a Norse name for an oak, transferred to other mountain trees.
Old English word for a mountain forest, given in explaining [[see:fir]].
Names both poison hemlock, which [[see:Socrates]] drank, and an unrelated nonpoisonous evergreen; 'hem' probably means poison, so the tree is unfairly named.
Drank poison [[see:hemlock]], the plant rather than the tree.
Named after [[from:Sequoyah]]; a variety of [[see:redwood]] and the largest one.
Cherokee innovator who created the Cherokee syllabary and improved relations with the US government; the [[see:sequoia]] is named after him.
A name applied to various trees over the years; the [[see:sequoia]] is the largest variety.
Wrongly named: means mulberry-leaved fig tree; what's now called a sycamore was a [[see:plane tree]] of genus [[see:Platanus]], confused with [[see:Acer]] maples.
Earlier name for what is now called a [[see:sycamore]]; called [[see:platane]] in France, where they line southern streets.
The genus of the [[see:plane tree]], with five-lobed leaves like [[see:Acer]].
The maple genus; its similar five-lobed leaves help explain naming crossover with [[see:sycamore]]s.
The French name for the [[equivalent:plane tree]], which lines streets in the south of France.
Its 'mul' comes from Latin [[from:morum]], a mulberry or blackberry, and is an example of a [[see:cranberry morpheme]].
A fossilised part of a compound word that isn't used on its own, common in berry and plant names like [[see:cranberry]] and [[see:raspberry]].
The 'cran' means crane, because the flower looks like a crane's head; it gives its name to the [[see:cranberry morpheme]].
Its 'rasp' isn't the grinding rasp but an older word for raspberry, so it means raspberry berry; not technically a berry.
Not technically a berry, with its seeds on the outside, as with [[see:raspberry]].
A true berry, unlike [[see:raspberry]].
From Cockney rhyming slang: raspberry tart rhymes with [[from:fart]].
Very old; found in an old Middle English translation of Aristotle describing farting by the [[see:fundament]], and possibly in [[see:partridge]].
Like [[same-root:fundamental]], the thing at the bottom, but also meant the anus, as in Middle English animal husbandry guides.
Related to [[same-root:fundament]], meaning the anus.
A fart bird, possibly from French [[from:péter (French)]], to fart, perhaps for its fluttering noise; related to [[same-root:petard]].
A little explosion, from the same French fart verb as [[same-root:partridge]].
From a Germanic word for root, from the same Indo-European root as Latin [[same-root:radix]].
Latin for root, sharing an Indo-European root with [[same-root:root]] and source of [[gave:radish]] and [[gave:radical]].
Related to [[same-root:radical]], so the hosts joke that early radicals were essentially radishes.
From [[from:radix]], root; originally like [[see:grassroots]], it took a political sense in the 1700s with calls for reform from the roots.
What [[see:radical]] originally meant, essentially.
British name for what Americans call beet; in Britain 'beet' might suggest [[see:sugar beet]].
A different type of beet, which British English 'beet' might suggest instead of [[see:beetroot]].
One of the mushrooms Jess has foraged in her neighbourhood.
A foraged mushroom, also called pheasant back, edible when young; contains [[see:dryad]] again.
Also called aborted entoloma: an entoloma that grows wrong and puffs up, becoming the safer edible form.
The nickname of the resinous polypore, which sounds better than its actual name.
Giant white basketball-sized mushroom that Jess hopes to find.
Small brown [[see:puffball]] growing on stumps, with a smooth marshmallowy inside; Rob finds 'stump' unappetising.
Simply Japanese for tree mushroom.
Means dancing mushroom; the same thing as [[equivalent:hen of the woods]].
Another name for [[equivalent:maitake]]; grows on the ground and looks feathered, not to be confused with [[see:chicken of the woods]].
A yellow mushroom named because it pulls apart like chicken, a good vegan alternative.
Large [[see:Agaricus bisporus]], named only about 40 years ago, perhaps for marketing; maybe from Italian [[from?:prataiolo]] or London's [[from?:Portobello Road]] market.
The unsexy original name for the [[see:portobello]], a large variety of it.
An Italian mushroom whose name [[see:portobello]] may be a folk-etymological corruption of.
London street with a market where the [[see:portobello]] may have been sold, giving it its name.
Contains neither mush nor room: a folk etymology of French [[from:mousseron]], related to [[same-root:moss]] and to an Old English word for bog.
The French word behind [[gave:mushroom]], once a general word for fungus; related to [[same-root:moss]], perhaps not to [[unrelated?:mousse]].
Related to [[same-root:mousseron]] and [[same-root:mushroom]].
Uncertainly related to [[see:mousseron]]; the dessert may instead come from Latin mulsus, mixed with honey, like [[same-root?:emulsion]] and [[same-root?:caramel]].
With emulsify, possibly related to [[same-root?:mousse]] through Latin mulsus.
Given as a possible relative of [[same-root?:mousse]].
Means squishy or spongy: via Latin, an adaptation of Greek [[from:spongos]], sponge.
For Jess mainly the red-and-white [[see:amanita]]; in England a thin stem with a flat top, something a toad might sit on.
Red-capped, white-spotted mushrooms that Jess associates with [[see:toadstool]]s, the showbiz mushroom of illustrations.
Its origin was discussed in an earlier episode.

entries.translation: thing that grows in a field
entries.note: French word for mushroom, sometimes used in English, meaning thing that grows in a field; compare [[same-root:Champagne]].
The French region, which gave champagne its name, comes from the word for countryside, as Jess guesses from [[same-root:champignon]].
Actually the same word as [[same-root:trifle]], both from words meaning trickery.
Same origin as [[same-root:truffle]], meaning a trick or frippery; a layered dessert named after something frivolous, like the [[see:fool]] and [[see:Eton mess]].
The brand name Americans use for jelly, a layer in a [[see:trifle]].
As in raspberry fool, a dessert named after something frivolous, like [[see:trifle]].
Another dessert named after something ridiculous, like [[see:trifle]].
Looks like hedge plus hog, but possibly a folk etymology of Slavic words related to [[same-root?:urchin]] and [[same-root?:igil]].
A word for a hedgehog in the 1300s, which is why a [[see:sea urchin]] is a sea hedgehog.
Basically a sea hedgehog, from [[from:urchin]].
French word briefly borrowed for a hedgehog, a variation on [[same-root:oursin]]; also the spiked part of a turnstile.
French for an urchin, of which [[same-root:hérisson]] is a variation.
Old English for hedgehog, meaning bristling; same as German Igel in [[see:Mettigel]], possibly from the same root as [[same-root?:urchin]].
Related to the bristling old French words for hedgehogs.
Named for its serrated leaves, from the same bristling root as old French hedgehog words.
A cursed German dish: raw spiced pork [[see:Mett]] shaped into a hedgehog with onion spikes; Igel matches Old English [[see:igil]].
Raw spiced pork mince, used to make a [[see:Mettigel]].
Danish or Norwegian for hedgehog: 'svin' means pig, like [[same-root:swine]], and 'pin' means spiky or stick.
The same as the pig element in [[same-root:pinsvin]].
Swedish for hedgehog, from igel, bristly, and a word for pine cone.
Originally meant a pine cone; the fruit was named for looking like one.
From a Native American word meaning head first, because it can run down a tree head first.
When a word's sound is reshaped into something easier for speakers to understand, as with [[see:dormouse]].
A Powhatan word meaning he scratches with the hands; elsewhere it's usually a wash bear, like German [[equivalent:Waschbär]].
German for [[equivalent:raccoon]], like many languages' wash-bear names.
Possibly badge-ard, for the blaze-like stripe on its head; Rob prefers an unverified theory from French [[from?:bêcher]], to dig.
In a different subfamily from the [[see:European badger]] and [[see:honey badger]]; Europeans probably named it for looking like their badger.
An Old World badger and a fierce fighter, hence its use in [[see:badger baiting]].
Disputed as a true badger; Jess finds it shares a subfamily with the [[see:European badger]] but not the [[see:American badger]].
A cruel blood sport that ended in England in the 1800s, source of the verb [[gave:badger]].
Not from badgers' behaviour but from the dogs' relentless attacks in [[from:badger baiting]].
Every sense comes from killing or injuring by biting and shaking the throat, so sheep worrying means killing sheep.
Means to grasp.
Refers to blades, meaning its claws.
Probably a shortening of [[from:mouldwarp]]; probably unrelated to [[unrelated?:mould]] and unrelated to the skin mark.
Middle English word for a mole meaning earth thrower, which gave [[gave:mole]] and the character [[see:Moldy Warp]].
A mole in the Little Grey Rabbit books, named after the old word [[from:mouldwarp]].
The fungus, probably not related to [[unrelated?:mole]].
Originally vole mouse, from an Old Norse word for field, so etymologically a field mouse.
The Old English word also meant muscle, as Latin's mouse word gave [[gave:muscle]].
From the Latin for a [[from:mouse]], since muscles look like mice running under the skin.
A [[see:folk etymology]] of a French word for a sleeper, for its long hibernation; explains the sleepy dormouse of Lewis Carroll.
Its first element comes from a word for chicken, because they stole chickens; Europeans also applied it to the [[see:skunk]].
A Native American word meaning roughly piss fox; Europeans called skunks [[see:polecat]]s.
Named as another animal like the [[see:skunk]] in this branch of mammals.
Related to [[same-root:hydra]], so it's a little sea monster; otters are rebounding, including near Birmingham's canals.
Related to [[same-root:otter]].
Means brown thing; once also a word for a warm fur hat, as beavers were hunted extensively for their fur.
